subject: Posterior fit for a many-term linear model

messages.author: 77e72e34bf8c033f
messages.subject: Posterior fit for a many-term linear model
parts:
Hi all,

I recently started using Stan and find it a wonderful tool, that I really enjoy using.

My model template looks something like this:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] x;
  int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
  real beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real y_tilde[N];
}
model {
  vector[N] mu;
  for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- alpha + beta * x[n]
  // in the real code there are many more contributions to mu, mu <- mu + new stuff
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  y_tilde ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

just a linear model with normal errors, where I use the y_tilde parameter to access to the posterior model fit.

The overhead in "resampling" for y_tilde means a ~ 2 x increase in runtime, which becomes a real issue for large models. I have searched the mailing list and other sources and as I understand it, the recommended approach for posterior predictions is to use the generated quantities, as

generated quantities {
   vector[N] y_tilde;
   y_tilde ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);
}

I guees my problem is that I add up a lot of contributions to the mean of the normal distribution  (mu which is a local variable in the model block), instead of writing the entire model in the likelihood line, y ~ normal(...), however this is how the R code generation wrapper is constructed and would be very time consuming to change. The fact that mu is a local variable in the model block, means that it cannot be accessed in the generated quantities or transformed parameters blocks. The obvious solution would be to regenerate the mu in the generated quantities block, but this I would rather avoid as it seems redundant.

I would really appreciate it if anyone could point me towards a solution/hack to solve my problem.

Also, I apologize if this has been discussed before.

Thanks,
Per

messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior fit for a many-term linear model
parts:
Hi Per,

Have you tried to use the generated quantities solution, which looks like:

generated quantities {
  vector[N] y_tilde;

for(n in 1:N)
    y_tilde[n] <- normal_rng(alpha + beta * x, sigma);
}

The generated quantities block as you have it written below won't work because there can't be '~' in generated quantities. Generated quantities is only evaluated after each NUTS iteration, whereas anything defined in the model block is evaluated (and differentiated) each leapfrog step, which is why you were seeing such a speed hit.


Rob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior fit for a many-term linear model
parts:
> On Feb 26, 2015, at 12:48 AM, Per Nielsen <evi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I recently started using Stan and find it a wonderful tool, that I really enjoy using.
>
> My model template looks something like this:
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N;
> vector[N] x;
> int<lower=0> y[N];
> }
> parameters {
> real alpha;
> real beta;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> real y_tilde[N];
> }
> model {
> vector[N] mu;
> for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- alpha + beta * x[n]
> // in the real code there are many more contributions to mu, mu <- mu + new stuff
> y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> y_tilde ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
I'd write this as:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] x;
int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
real alpha;
real beta;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model {
y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
real y_tilde[N];
for (n in 1:N)

y_tilde[N] <- normal_rng(alpha + beta * x[n], sigma);
}

First, the alpha + beta * x construction will be a
bit more efficient (not because of the loop, but because
the gradients for alpha can be shared.

Second, recomputing mu in the generated quantities block is
super cheap as no gradients are involved.

Third, it will be more efficiently statstically because you
get proper Monte Carlo samples, not just MCMC ones.

As of yet, there's no way to vectorize the normal_rng
function. What I'd like to allow is just

normal_rng(alpha + beta * x); // ILLEGAL in Stan 2.6

If the calculation of mu is much more complex, then I'd
suggest storing it in the transformed parameters block, where
it will be available.

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] x;
int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
real alpha;
real beta;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}

transformed parameters {
vector[N] mu;
mu <- alpha + beta * x;
}
model {
y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
real y_tilde[N];
for (n in 1:N)

y_tilde[N] <- normal_rng(mu[n], sigma);
}

You can suppress saving the mu values in RStan, but not in CmdStan.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior fit for a many-term linear model
parts: Yes, it's done internally in the RNG

> On Feb 26, 2015, at 1:59 AM, Per Nielsen <evi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Rob and Bob


> Thank you both for your very fast answers!
>
> I will have a closer look at the transformed parameters block, and then I might as well use the "Matt trick" while I'm at it :)

The "Matt trick" is the non-centered parameterization if you
want to look it up in the literature.
> Btw, why isn't the "Matt trick" done internally in the rng? For me it seems like a pretty simple mapping.

Yes, it's the way the RNG works, but not how sampling works.

Sampling operates on the unconstrained parameter space, which
is defined by the constraints on the parameters --- each is mapped
to unconstrained support and the appropriate Jacobian adjustment
is applied to maintain the right sampling. There's a chapter
detailing the exact transforms in the manual.

- Bob
